speaker: PROF. ALFORD
text: appropriate ways to reduce the price of goods and services. The question is how.

speaker: PROF. ALFORD
text: When we think of consumer spending, credit card swipe fees are not the first thing that comes to mind. Yet those fees are a surprisingly large part of consumer spending. Last year, the average American spent $1 ,100 in swipe fees, more than they spent on pets, coffee, or alcohol. And I would ask you, which of those four are you least likely, at least excited to be paying for?

speaker: PROF. ALFORD
text: When we think of consumer, my message today is simple. Given the importance of the economy to voters in the last election, I'm

speaker: SEN. DURBIN
text: like shrieking, scalded cats when I hear about consumer competition on credit cards. Why does it scare the living hell out of them? Because they make so much money off them right now. Well, is the converse true with this regulation and this competition when it comes to interchange fees change the equation so much that they couldn't be profitable?

speaker: SEN. DURBIN
text: I use as an illustration the fact that the credit cards are regulated in Europe and the interchange fee is capped at 0 .3 percent. Try to remember that number for a moment. 0 .3 percent interchange fee in Europe for Visa and MasterCard and those who participate in that. What is it in the United States? 1 to 3 percent.

speaker: SEN. DURBIN
text: Well, basic math, what you're saying is in the United States, the interchange fee is 3 to 10 times as much as it is in Europe.

speaker: SEN. DURBIN
text: How do they get by with that? How can Visa and MasterCard possibly survive with such a difference contrast?

speaker: SEN. DURBIN
text: The bottom line, of course, is that they are profitable in Europe even when restricted to 0 .3 percent in interchange fees. And it also is very clear that when it comes to these interchange fees and the frequent flyer programs, they're still offering them in Europe.

speaker: SEN. DURBIN
text: So to me, as I sit here and take a look at the situation, the obvious question I ask Mr. Sheedy is how can you possibly do business in Europe when the interchange fee is restricted at a maximum of 0 .3 percent?

speaker: MR. SHEEDY
text: Thank you, Senator Durbin.

speaker: MR. SHEEDY
text: You're correct.

speaker: MR. SHEEDY
text: The European government did regulate interchange rates in Europe. The government in Europe imposed a fixed interchange fee and it did impact the market.

speaker: MR. SHEEDY
text: But you're correct that there are some reward programs in Europe. The majority of them were either eliminated or greatly devalued.

speaker: MR. SHEEDY
text: Consumer rewards, which are enjoyed by 84 percent of U .S. cardholders today, so it's a broad spectrum, broad socioeconomic spectrum of U .S. consumers enjoy rewards. That is not the case in Europe where reward programs have been reduced, fees to consumers have gone up.

speaker: MR. SHEEDY
text: You're correct, the market adjusted, but ultimately we think that those changes that happened in Europe were bad for European consumers and European cardholders.

speaker: SEN. DURBIN
text: Let me ask you a question about an individual.

speaker: SEN. DURBIN
text: Are you familiar with Mr. Prabhu, Mr. Sheedy?

speaker: MR. SHEEDY
text: Yes, he used to be the chief financial officer of Visa.

speaker: SEN. DURBIN
text: He said, net net, we are a beneficiary of inflation. Visa was a beneficiary. How is that possible?

speaker: MR. SHEEDY
text: I don't think of Visa as being a beneficiary of Visa, of inflation, excuse me.

speaker: MR. SHEEDY
text: It's impossible for me to know the context within which.

speaker: SEN. DURBIN
text: So let me read a larger part of the quote. To the extent that there's inflation driving up ticket size, clearly it's beneficial to us, he said, on behalf of Visa, so net net, I mean we are a beneficiary of inflation.

speaker: SEN. DURBIN
text: So while American families are struggling to survive against inflation, you're doing quite well, as long as the ticket size goes up and your percentage applies, correct?

speaker: MR. SHEEDY
text: I don't believe that inflation is good for our business or anyone's business. I think a healthy economy is best for the U .S. consumer, U .S. merchants, and when U .S. merchants and U .S. consumers come together and transact, that drives transactions on our network. That's what we want, and that's how we think about growing the business.

speaker: SEN. DURBIN
text: Well, I can tell you that the CFO of your company, January 27, 2022, at a different point of view and one that makes more sense.

speaker: SEN. DURBIN
text: You're in a situation where you're benefiting from the weakness in our economy and the fact that it's impacted Mr. Callahan, as well as families and consumers. What we're trying to do here is to do something you said you favor. Competition benefits everyone.

speaker: SEN. DURBIN
text: Why not some competition for Visa and MasterCard?

speaker: SEN. DURBIN
text: Senator Graham.

speaker: SEN. GRAHAM
text: Thank you, Mr. Chairman. It's been a very informative hearing, and I will ask simple questions because that's all I know how to do here.

speaker: SEN. GRAHAM
text: So, simple question.

speaker: SEN. GRAHAM
text: The rates in Europe are by regulations, is that right, Mr. Sheedy?

speaker: MR. SHEEDY
text: Yes, Senator.

speaker: SEN. GRAHAM
text: The argument is that rates are high here because we have a monopoly, no competition. Is that right, Mr. Cantor?

speaker: MR. KANTOR
text: That's right.

speaker: SEN. GRAHAM
text: Okay. So, you agree with me, Europe doesn't use competition to get rates down. They use regulation.

speaker: SEN. GRAHAM
text: Are you proposing we use regulation or competition?

speaker: MR. KANTOR
text: We're proposing competition. That's what's in the bill.

speaker: SEN. GRAHAM
text: And there's no data about what competition does yet, right?

speaker: MR. KANTOR
text: Actually, there is because in many places around the world, they do have that competition on credit cards. So, France, Denmark, South Korea, also several of the debit systems, including in the U .S. and Canada, have competition as well.

speaker: SEN. GRAHAM
text: For credit cards?

speaker: MR. KANTOR
text: So, that's on debit, but in Europe and Korea, it's

speaker: SEN. GRAHAM
text: on credit. Okay. So, here's my point. We've got two systems here. We've got a regulatory system that reduces cost to consumers, and Mr. Alford, you say in Europe it actually does benefit the consumer.

speaker: SEN. GRAHAM
text: There are lower exchange fees.

speaker: PROF. ALFORD
text: The lower exchange fees do benefit consumers with respect to the price of goods and services because 70 percent…

speaker: SEN. GRAHAM
text: Okay. The question is, if you lower their cost, would it matter to you, the consumer? At least in Europe, the answer is yes.

speaker: PROF. ALFORD
text: Can you repeat the question?

speaker: SEN. GRAHAM
text: At least in Europe, the answer is yes. The regulation has lowered cost to consumers.

speaker: PROF. ALFORD
text: Yes. The regulation in Europe has…

speaker: SEN. GRAHAM
text: And in theory, competition would lower cost here.

speaker: PROF. ALFORD
text: Yes. I mean, I…

speaker: SEN. GRAHAM
text: Do you prefer competition or regulation of the fees?

speaker: PROF. ALFORD
text: I prefer competition, and I think that the…

speaker: SEN. GRAHAM
text: Does anybody prefer regulation?

speaker: MR. KANTOR
text: Okay. Well, regulation can be pro -competitive, of course.

speaker: SEN. GRAHAM
text: Yeah, but I mean, we don't have any.

speaker: MR. KANTOR
text: The proposal is to not have price caps… You know, the proposal is to create competition.

speaker: SEN. GRAHAM
text: Through… Right?

speaker: MR. KANTOR
text: Through routing restrictions. Exactly.

speaker: SEN. GRAHAM
text: So, Senator Durbin's not proposing regulation. He's proposing competition. Is that correct?

speaker: MR. KANTOR
text: Yes.

speaker: MR. KANTOR
text: Introducing…

speaker: SEN. GRAHAM
text: And we know in Europe, the swipe fees are cheaper, right?

speaker: SEN. GRAHAM
text: And you tell us, Mr. Alford, in Europe, the consumer benefits.

speaker: PROF. ALFORD
text: Studies, independent studies, revealed that there is significant pass -through, yes.

speaker: SEN. GRAHAM
text: Okay. And you say, Mr. Shih, that consumers in Europe get less rewards. Is that correct?

speaker: MR. SHEEDY
text: Their fees are higher, and they get fewer rewards.

speaker: SEN. GRAHAM
text: Are their fees higher than yours?

speaker: MR. SHEEDY
text: I'm referring, Senator, to the fees that are being charged by the banks.

speaker: SEN. GRAHAM
text: No, no, no, no, no. The swipe fees in Europe are regulated at what?

speaker: MR. SHEEDY
text: Point three.

speaker: SEN. GRAHAM
text: Correct. Okay. And what are your swipe fees?

speaker: MR. SHEEDY
text: The average interchange fee in the United States on credit is approximately two percent.

speaker: SEN. GRAHAM
text: Okay. Again, this is simple. Two percent is bigger than zero point three, I think, right?

speaker: MR. SHEEDY
text: Yes.

speaker: SEN. GRAHAM
text: Okay. Thanks. So, here we are.

speaker: SEN. GRAHAM
text: What I'm trying to figure out is, should I do a regulatory approach?

speaker: SEN. GRAHAM
text: Because nobody really can tell me what competition is going to do. I know what regulation has done over there. Now what I want to do is figure out, what do you lose if you regulate? So, Ms. Kirkpatrick, what kind of reward programs are offered?

speaker: SEN. GRAHAM
text: You get reward. What kind of stuff do you get?

speaker: MS. KIRKPATRICK
text: The reward programs. Senator, there's a variety of reward

speaker: SEN. GRAHAM
text: programs. Well, name a few.

speaker: MS. KIRKPATRICK
text: Which range from cash back to rewards for travel to rewards for everyday purchases like gas and grocery.

speaker: SEN. GRAHAM
text: Okay. So, lower income people can participate in this reward program.

speaker: MS. KIRKPATRICK
text: Yes, greater than 80 percent of cardholders in the United States can benefit from these rewards.

speaker: SEN. GRAHAM
text: So, Mr. Kantor, you say that most low income people kind of don't, they get left out here, right?

speaker: MR. KANTOR
text: They pay more in the fees and much more of the rewards go to the high income folks. That's according to the Federal Reserve.

speaker: SEN. GRAHAM
text: Okay. Do you agree with that, Ms. Kirkpatrick?

speaker: MS. KIRKPATRICK
text: I agree that 80 percent or more of cardholders in the

speaker: SEN. GRAHAM
text: U .S. No, that's not the question. Do you agree with what the Federal Reserve said?

speaker: MS. KIRKPATRICK
text: I agree with the fact that rewards are widely

speaker: SEN. GRAHAM
text: evaluated. No, it's a simple question. Do you agree with what the Federal Reserve analysis was?

speaker: MS. KIRKPATRICK
text: I haven't seen that particular analysis.

speaker: SEN. GRAHAM
text: Well, you need to look at it. So, here's my deal. I'm very open minded to the solution.

speaker: SEN. GRAHAM
text: I generally like competition except when they're monopolies.

speaker: SEN. GRAHAM
text: The whole idea of regulation is to make sure that in a capitalist society, water is in the bank. It doesn't overflow.

speaker: SEN. GRAHAM
text: I don't know exactly how I'm going to come out, but you're having a hard time convincing me that the fees here are set to the advantage of the consumer.

speaker: SEN. GRAHAM
text: Thanks.

speaker: THE CHAIR
text: Thanks, Senator Graham. Senator Coons.

speaker: THE CHAIR
text: Information that's out there. So, thank you. Thanks, Senator Klobuchar. Senator Kennedy.

speaker: SEN. KENNEDY
text: Thank you, Mr. Chairman.

speaker: SEN. KENNEDY
text: Mr. Sheedy, you're our Senior Advisor to the Visa CEO?

speaker: MR. SHEEDY
text: Yes, sir.

speaker: SEN. KENNEDY
text: The Visa CEO was too busy to come today?

speaker: MR. SHEEDY
text: He had a conflict, Senator.

speaker: MR. SHEEDY
text: He knows that I enjoyed speaking with this committee two years ago and that I was looking forward to coming back. But he, unfortunately, was not able to be here today.

speaker: SEN. KENNEDY
text: What was his conflict?

speaker: MR. SHEEDY
text: I honestly don't know what his conflict was, but I know he was unable to be here today.

speaker: SEN. KENNEDY
text: But it was more important that he be somewhere else than here.

speaker: MR. SHEEDY
text: He was unable to be here today. He sends his regards.

speaker: SEN. KENNEDY
text: Send them right back to him.

speaker: SEN. KENNEDY
text: Look, I don't, if we had to vote on this bill today, I don't know how I would vote.

speaker: SEN. KENNEDY
text: But I want to thank the Chairman for calling this hearing. I've learned a lot today.

speaker: SEN. KENNEDY
text: I've just got a couple of questions and then an observation.

speaker: SEN. KENNEDY
text: Professor, you seem to be fairly objective here.

speaker: SEN. KENNEDY
text: Congress capped the fees on debit cards, is that correct?

speaker: PROF. ALFORD
text: That's correct, for certain transactions, yes.

speaker: SEN. KENNEDY
text: The savings, has it been passed on to the consumer and or invested in the retailer's business?

speaker: PROF. ALFORD
text: Yes, so the rate, the average rate for...

speaker: SEN. KENNEDY
text: Give me, I don't speak Sanskrit.

speaker: PROF. ALFORD
text: Yes, the answer is yes.

speaker: SEN. KENNEDY
text: I need short answers. Is that a yes or a no?

speaker: PROF. ALFORD
text: Yes.

speaker: SEN. KENNEDY
text: And we addressed the issue in debit cards by regulating, we capped the fees. This bill doesn't cap fees like they do in Europe, as Senator Graham so eloquently pointed out. This bill just introduces competition.

speaker: PROF. ALFORD
text: That's correct.

speaker: SEN. KENNEDY
text: All right, I really came today to watch Senator Hawley and to learn, but here's my observation. I'm going to cede my time to Senator Hawley. Let me just say this to all of you, but particularly our friends at Visa and MasterCard. And I mean it, I don't know how I would vote if this bill came up today.

speaker: SEN. KENNEDY
text: Visa and MasterCard and the folks, the retailers, need to sit down and work this out.

speaker: SEN. KENNEDY
text: You need to sit down and work this out.

speaker: SEN. KENNEDY
text: Because if you don't, Congress is going to do something. I'm not sure what we're going to do.

speaker: SEN. KENNEDY
text: But Visa and MasterCard, when we get through with you, you could end up looking like either the post office or the Dallas Cowboys.

speaker: SEN. KENNEDY
text: I'm not sure we'll get it right. And I'm not a big fan of the European model, that we're seeing the cost right now in Europe of their pension for regulation.

speaker: SEN. KENNEDY
text: But what I do care is the fact that the high prices in this country are gutting the American people like a fish.

speaker: SEN. KENNEDY
text: And we're trying to address it. And my strong advice to you is to sit down and try to work this out.

speaker: SEN. KENNEDY
text: And come up with a solution that's fair for the consumer, fair for the retailer, but also respects Visa and MasterCard. You're two great companies and I appreciate that.

speaker: SEN. KENNEDY
text: But something's not adding up here.

speaker: SEN. KENNEDY
text: And next time, Mr. Sheedy, it's wonderful to see you. Ask your CEO to come.

speaker: SEN. KENNEDY
text: I know he's a busy, important man, but ask him to come.

speaker: SEN. WELCH
text: You know what? I think competition then is going to put the pressure on the others.

speaker: SEN. WELCH
text: I want to talk about another thing.

speaker: SEN. WELCH
text: The rates that you charge merchants vary. What do you charge Walmart?

speaker: MR. SHEEDY
text: We have a large business with Walmart.

speaker: SEN. WELCH
text: What do you charge Walmart?

speaker: SEN. WELCH
text: Level it. Let's be candid and transparent instead of rhetorical. What do you charge Walmart?

speaker: MR. SHEEDY
text: Senator, as I sit here, I don't know what the Walmart rates

speaker: SEN. WELCH
text: are. What do you charge Mr. Callahan?

speaker: SEN. WELCH
text: Mr. Kirkpatrick, what do you charge Walmart?

speaker: MS. KIRKPATRICK
text: I don't have the information.

speaker: SEN. WELCH
text: What do you charge Mr. Callahan?

speaker: MS. KIRKPATRICK
text: I would have to -

speaker: SEN. WELCH
text: Well, you both negotiate with Walmart, right? Because they're big.

speaker: MS. KIRKPATRICK
text: Walmart's a big customer.

speaker: SEN. WELCH
text: If Mr. Callahan wants to get the Walmart deal, does he have your phone number or know how to get it and call you up and say, hey, let's make a deal?

speaker: SEN. WELCH
text: We're having tough times here in Cambridge and I want to keep selling books to my community. Can he call you?

speaker: SEN. WELCH
text: Can he call you?

speaker: MS. KIRKPATRICK
text: I would welcome the opportunity to talk to Mr. Callahan and connect him to third parties that can help him

speaker: SEN. WELCH
text: exercise his rights. How many millions of Mr. Callahans do you have?

speaker: MS. KIRKPATRICK
text: There are 33 million U .S. businesses.

speaker: SEN. WELCH
text: Right. So do you have a business unit where you have lots of people who can handle 33 million accounts like Mr. Callahan's who call you up? You talked, Mr. Sheehy, you talked about how you know the customer. What about the merchant?

speaker: SEN. WELCH
text: They're getting so ripped off, so ripped off.

speaker: SEN. WELCH
text: Where's that chart here? You know, this is another issue.

speaker: SEN. WELCH
text: Three -tenths of a percent in -person cap in the EU, right?

speaker: SEN. WELCH
text: Visa does business, right, in the EU?

speaker: MR. SHEEDY
text: Yes.

speaker: SEN. WELCH
text: And MasterCard does business in the EU, right?

speaker: MS. KIRKPATRICK
text: Yes.

speaker: SEN. WELCH
text: And all of those wonderful things you described, fraud protection, consumer confidence, you do that in Europe just like you do here in the United States, right?

speaker: MR. SHEEDY
text: Yes.

speaker: SEN. WELCH
text: So why not have Mr. Callahan pay the lower rate and all of Mr. Callahan's around the country?

speaker: SEN. WELCH
text: What's the problem? You're able to do it and make a profit?

speaker: MR. SHEEDY
text: Senator, we share your values in wanting to drive lower prices for small businesses.

speaker: SEN. WELCH
text: You are killing small business in the United States of America.

speaker: SEN. WELCH
text: I yield back.

speaker: THE CHAIR
text: Senator Tillis.

text: Thank you, Mr. Chairman. I sometimes try to solve it because I'll guarantee you the solution coming from Congress will not be good for anyone.

text: Thank you, Mr. Chair. Senator Hawley. Thank you, Mr. Chairman. Just on the point about Visa and MasterCard being successful businesses, I think you've figured it out, haven't you? I mean, what's your profit margin, Ms. Kirkpatrick?

text: It's circa 50%.

text: Mr. Sheedy?

text: Slightly higher.

text: Higher than 50 % profit margin?

text: Slightly higher than MasterCard, yes.

text: That's incredible. 50 % profit margin. I mean, that's absolutely unbelievable. What's the answer to the Walmart question, by the way, that Senator Welch posed to you? What's Walmart's interchange fee that you negotiate with them?
